headline_insight: While overall insurance comprehension is similar across genders, a significantly higher percentage of female clients report a very poor understanding of their coverage compared to male clients, highlighting a critical gap in basic insurance literacy.
paragraphs: According to the 2026 Insurance Survey, there is a distinct gender gap in the lowest levels of insurance literacy, with 10.4% of female clients (158 out of 1,518) reporting a 'very poor' understanding of their insurance coverage compared to only 5.6% of male clients (33 out of 586). This 4.8 percentage point difference is statistically significant, whereas the differences in other comprehension categories—such as the 39.7% of females and 42.8% of males who report a 'good' understanding—do not show statistical significance. Similarly, for the claims process, 11.5% of female clients (175 out of 1,518) and 7.3% of male clients (43 out of 586) report a 'very poor' understanding, representing a difference of 4.2 percentage points that is not statistically significant. Benchmark data is not available for these indicators to compare these levels of understanding against broader market standards. These findings imply that VisionFund must design targeted, gender-sensitive educational interventions specifically aimed at women who are completely excluded from understanding their coverage, ensuring they are not left behind in basic insurance literacy.

When examining how clients prefer to receive information, in-person communication channels are overwhelmingly the most effective. Specifically, 59.4% of female clients (901 out of 1,518) and 60.9% of male clients (357 out of 586) identify in-person explanations from MFI staff or loan officers as effective, while group meetings are valued by 56.4% of females (856 out of 1,518) and 56.7% of males (332 out of 586). In contrast, digital channels like SMS or WhatsApp messages are considered effective by only 11.9% of females and 14.8% of males, and printed materials are effective for just 2.1% of females and 4.1% of males. Qualitative insights reinforce the value of localized, face-to-face communication, particularly through group leadership; for example, a female client in Uganda explained that her primary source of information was 'The chairperson of the group,' while another female client in Uganda simply identified 'The group chairperson.' A male client in Uganda similarly noted relying on 'some group members' for information. Benchmark data is not available for these communication channel indicators. For VisionFund's programming, this highlights the critical importance of leveraging existing group structures and training group chairpersons to act as information hubs, rather than relying on digital or print campaigns which have very low reach.

The survey data also reveals that household disability status does not result in statistically significant differences in insurance comprehension. For instance, 39.2% of clients in households with persons with disabilities (PWD HH, 187 out of 477) report a 'good' understanding of coverage, compared to 41.0% of clients in non-PWD households (665 out of 1,621). Regarding the claims process, 37.1% of PWD HH clients (177 out of 477) and 41.1% of non-PWD HH clients (667 out of 1,621) report a 'good' understanding, which is not a statistically significant difference. Benchmark data is not available for these disability-disaggregated indicators. Although the lack of significant differences suggests that clients from PWD households are not experiencing worse access to information than their peers, the absolute levels of poor understanding remain high across both groups—with 23.5% of PWD HH clients and 20.9% of non-PWD HH clients reporting a 'poor' understanding of the claims process. This implies that VisionFund's product design and training modules must be universally accessible and simplified to improve overall comprehension for all clients, regardless of disability status.
